topic: Safe withdrawal of long-term prednisolone in adults
page_contents_html:
Safe withdrawal of long-term prednisolone in adults

Use this guide for adults taking prednisolone for a non-endocrine condition when the underlying disease is controlled and treatment is no longer required. It applies particularly after prednisolone 5 mg daily or more for 4 weeks or longer.

Key principles

  • Do not stop long-term prednisolone abruptly. Reduce higher doses more quickly, then use smaller reductions and longer intervals near the physiological dose of 4-6 mg daily.
  • Only start the final withdrawal when the condition being treated is controlled. A disease-specific or specialist taper takes precedence.
  • Routine adrenal testing is not required while the patient remains on a supraphysiological dose or still needs prednisolone for disease control.
  • At 5 mg daily or below, regard the patient as potentially adrenal-suppressed until recovery is demonstrated. Provide sick-day advice and ensure they have a Steroid Emergency Card.

accordion_sections.heading: Who this guide is for
accordion_sections.html:
Use this guide when all of the following apply

  • The patient is an adult and is not pregnant.
  • Prednisolone was prescribed for a non-endocrine condition.
  • The patient has usually taken 5 mg daily or more for 4 weeks or longer.
  • The underlying condition is controlled and prednisolone is no longer required, or a reduction has been agreed with the clinician managing that condition.

Do not use this guide alone for

  • Known primary, secondary or tertiary adrenal insufficiency, pituitary disease or glucocorticoid replacement therapy
  • Pregnancy, children or young people
  • A condition with its own treatment-specific taper, including a plan supplied by the initiating specialist
  • Patients who still require prednisolone to control the underlying disease

Before reducing the dose

  • Confirm the indication, current dose, duration and previous attempts to reduce or stop.
  • Check for recent repeated oral courses and concurrent inhaled, topical, intra-articular, intramuscular or intranasal corticosteroids. Risk is cumulative across routes.
  • Check for medicines that increase glucocorticoid exposure, particularly strong CYP3A4 inhibitors.
  • Assess current disease activity and agree what would indicate a relapse.
  • Explain that fatigue, nausea, muscle or joint pain and low mood can occur during withdrawal and may overlap with adrenal insufficiency or recurrence of the underlying condition.

accordion_sections.heading: Suggested prednisolone taper
accordion_sections.html:
This is a starting framework for a patient whose underlying condition is controlled. Individualise the pace according to treatment duration, previous withdrawal symptoms, comorbidity, glucocorticoid complications and risk of disease flare.

Current daily doseSuggested reductionInterval
More than 40 mgReduce by 5-10 mgEvery week
20-40 mgReduce by 5 mgEvery week
10-20 mgReduce by 2.5 mgEvery 1-4 weeks
5-10 mgReduce by 1 mgEvery 1-4 weeks
5 mgIf clinically well, reduce by 1 mg. Alternatively assess HPA-axis recovery as described below.Every 4 weeks

Practical points

  • Prescribe the dose once daily in the morning unless the condition-specific plan states otherwise.
  • Review before each reduction once the dose reaches 5 mg daily.
  • Do not routinely switch prednisolone to hydrocortisone. A switch may be considered if small prednisolone reductions are not practicable or on specialist advice.
  • If rapid reduction is required because of serious glucocorticoid toxicity, discuss the balance between disease control and adrenal risk with the relevant specialist.

accordion_sections.heading: At 5 mg daily: clinical taper or adrenal testing
accordion_sections.html:
At a physiological-equivalent dose, either continue a slow clinical taper or use a morning serum cortisol if confirmation of HPA-axis recovery is needed. Most patients do not need a short Synacthen test routinely.

Continue a clinical taper

If the patient is clinically well and the underlying condition remains controlled, reduce by 1 mg every 4 weeks. Monitor for adrenal insufficiency, glucocorticoid withdrawal and disease flare.

Consider testing when

  • Stopping without a prolonged final taper is being considered
  • Symptoms suggest possible adrenal insufficiency during the final taper
  • Confirmation of HPA-axis recovery is needed before elective surgery or another significant physiological stress
  • The clinical taper has stalled or the diagnosis remains uncertain

How to arrange a morning cortisol

  • Test only after the dose has reached 5 mg daily or below.
  • Collect serum cortisol between 8 am and 9 am, before that day's prednisolone dose.
  • Follow current D&G laboratory instructions on how long prednisolone must be withheld because assay interference and local methods vary. Give the delayed dose immediately after sampling unless advised otherwise.

Proposed local interpretation - confirm before publication

The thresholds below reproduce the supplied NHS D&G draft and the NHS GGC 2024 protocol. They require confirmation by NHS D&G Endocrinology and Biochemistry for the local cortisol assay and short Synacthen test procedure.

ResultMorning cortisolPost-Synacthen cortisolAction
No recoveryBelow 100 nmol/LBelow 250 nmol/LDo not reduce further. Continue physiological cover and reassess in 2 months.
Partial recovery100-300 nmol/L250-430 nmol/LStart or continue the slow taper with safety-netting.
RecoveryAbove 300 nmol/LAbove 430 nmol/LPrednisolone can be stopped if the underlying disease remains controlled.

Arrange a short Synacthen test only through the agreed local pathway or after endocrine advice. Dynamic-test thresholds are assay-dependent.

accordion_sections.heading: Symptoms during the taper
accordion_sections.html:
At each review distinguish between

Possible problemTypical cluesAction
Glucocorticoid withdrawalFatigue, malaise, nausea, muscle or joint pain, sleep disturbance or mood change; may occur while the dose is still supraphysiological.If symptoms are severe, return temporarily to the most recent tolerated dose, reassess and resume with smaller reductions or longer intervals.
Adrenal insufficiencyFatigue, nausea, weakness, poor appetite, weight loss, postural dizziness or hypotension; risk becomes clinically important near or below the physiological dose or during acute illness.Pause the taper, assess promptly and ensure stress-dose cover when indicated. Seek endocrine advice if symptoms persist or the diagnosis is uncertain.
Underlying disease flareReturn of disease-specific symptoms, signs or inflammatory markers.Follow the condition-specific plan or contact the clinician managing the underlying disease. Do not continue reducing solely to complete the schedule.

These conditions overlap and may coexist. Review the timing of symptoms in relation to dose reductions, current dose, examination and disease-specific findings rather than relying on symptoms alone.

accordion_sections.heading: Sick-day rules and emergency action
accordion_sections.html:
During the final taper

  • At 5 mg daily or below, regard the patient as potentially adrenal-suppressed until HPA-axis recovery has been demonstrated.
  • Issue an NHS Steroid Emergency Card and provide written sick-day advice.
  • Tell the patient to show the card whenever they are acutely unwell, injured, admitted to hospital or having surgery or an invasive procedure.
  • Patients with current or recent glucocorticoid exposure whose adrenal recovery has not been confirmed require stress-dose cover during significant illness or procedures. Follow the current local sick-day and peri-operative guidance.

Suspected adrenal crisis

Consider adrenal crisis in a patient with current or recent prednisolone exposure who develops haemodynamic instability, collapse, confusion, persistent vomiting or diarrhoea, severe weakness, abdominal pain or hypoglycaemia.

Arrange emergency assessment immediately. Do not delay treatment for diagnostic testing. Give parenteral hydrocortisone and intravenous fluid resuscitation in accordance with the current adrenal-crisis protocol.

After prednisolone is stopped, continue steroid-card and sick-day precautions for the period specified in the locally approved policy unless HPA-axis recovery has been demonstrated. Adrenal suppression may persist after treatment ends.

accordion_sections.heading: When to seek specialist advice
accordion_sections.html:
Most adults tapering prednisolone for a non-endocrine condition do not require routine Endocrinology referral.

Contact the clinician managing the underlying disease when

  • The disease is not controlled or flares during dose reduction
  • The indication, treatment target or disease-specific taper is unclear
  • Serious glucocorticoid toxicity requires a faster reduction

Seek Endocrinology advice when

  • There is a history of adrenal crisis
  • HPA-axis recovery has not occurred after 1 year at a physiological-equivalent dose
  • Symptoms suggesting adrenal insufficiency persist despite pausing the taper or returning to the last tolerated physiological dose
  • Morning cortisol results are discordant with the clinical picture, a short Synacthen test is being considered, or interpretation is uncertain
  • There is suspected pituitary, hypothalamic or primary adrenal disease
  • A peri-operative or acute-illness steroid plan cannot be safely determined from current local guidance

notes_for_editor: This is a prescribing and patient-safety guide, so the accordion headings intentionally do not use the standard referral-pathway structure.
Confirm the morning cortisol and post-Synacthen thresholds with NHS D&G Endocrinology and Biochemistry before publication; cortisol interpretation is assay-dependent.
Confirm the locally required prednisolone washout before morning cortisol testing and the approved route for arranging a short Synacthen test.
Confirm the D&G sick-day dosing, peri-operative guidance, Steroid Emergency Card supply process and duration of precautions after prednisolone cessation.
